reason: The sources corroborate dozens of specific, surprising facts across multiple independent outlets regarding Stardust's aerogel collection, trajectory, Utah landing, and citizen science findings.
story: In 1999, NASA launched Stardust on a seven-year, nearly three-billion-mile journey to capture dust from a comet. Because particles colliding at thousands of miles per hour would vaporize on contact with ordinary surfaces, engineers deployed a tennis-racket-shaped collector packed with ultra-low-density aerogel—a porous substance that is 99.8 percent empty space. In January 2004, Stardust flew past Comet Wild 2, gently braking microscopic cometary grains and passing interstellar dust without destroying them. On January 15, 2006, its sample return capsule detached and parachuted safely into the Utah desert, completing the first mission ever to return comet samples to Earth. While the mothership was redirected to photograph Comet Tempel 1, tens of thousands of online citizen scientists searched digital microscope images of the aerogel, successfully uncovering organic molecules and seven rare grains of interstellar dust older than our Solar System.
angle: To catch cometary particles flying at thousands of miles per hour without destroying them, NASA trapped them inside aerogel—a porous substance that is 99.8 percent empty space.

claims.claim: NASA launched the robotic space probe Stardust on February 7, 1999.
Stardust was the first spacecraft to collect and return samples from a comet to Earth.
Stardust flew by the asteroid 5535 Annefrank on November 2, 2002.
Stardust encountered Comet Wild 2 in January 2004.
The spacecraft used ultra-low-density silica aerogel to capture dust particles without destroying them.
The collector tray deployed to capture particles was shaped like a tennis racket and provided about 1,000 square centimeters of collection surface.
On January 15, 2006, at 05:57 UT/UTC, the Sample Return Capsule successfully separated from the mothership.
Approximately four hours after separating from the spacecraft, the sample capsule entered Earth's atmosphere on January 15, 2006.
The sample capsule descended under parachutes and touched down in the Utah desert at the Utah Test and Training Range.
The probe covered an interplanetary journey of roughly 2.9 to 3 billion miles over seven years before delivering the samples.
The returned sample container was sent to NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas, for analysis.
After releasing the capsule, the Stardust mothership conducted an avoidance maneuver and was put into hibernation on January 29, 2006.
In July 2007, NASA approved an extended mission for the spacecraft called NExT to fly past Comet Tempel 1.
Stardust encountered Comet Tempel 1 on February 15, 2011, at a distance of 181 kilometers.
On March 24, 2011, Stardust carried out a final burn to consume its remaining fuel and sent its final transmission.
The citizen science project Stardust@home allowed members of the public to hunt for microscopic dust tracks using virtual microscope software.
In 2014, scientists announced the identification of seven probable interstellar dust particles captured in the aerogel.
Stardust@home volunteer Bruce Hudson found an aerogel track containing an interstellar grain that he named Orion.
Scientific analysis of the returned cometary dust confirmed the presence of a wide variety of organic compounds.

disputed: Closest approach distance to Comet Wild 2: S1 states 237 km, S5 states 236 km, and S2 states 250 km (155 miles). Scripts should state approximately 240 to 250 kilometers.
Capsule touchdown time: S1 and S5 report touchdown at 10:12 UT/GMT, while S2 reports 10:10 UT. Scripts should state around 10:10 to 10:12 UTC.

First mission to return extraterrestrial samples beyond lunar orbit: S4 notes Stardust was the first NASA sample return mission since Apollo, while S2 clarifies it was the second designed to return samples from beyond lunar orbit, following Genesis. Scripts should focus specifically on Stardust being the first to return samples from a comet.

Announcement timing of the seven interstellar dust grains: S1 mentions both April and August 2014, S4 specifies April 2014, and S2 specifies August 2014. Scripts should attribute the announcement generally to 2014.
